source: Verleger, Rose, Wagner, Yordanova, Kolev (2013) Insights into sleep's role for insight: studies with the number reduction task (reports Wagner et al. 2004 Experiment 1 in full)
finding: Gives the exact Wagner 2004 numbers. After an 8-hour night of sleep, more participants found the hidden shortcut than in any of four control groups. The authors state a base rate of about 20-25 percent insight without sleep, and an extra 30-40 percent from sleep.
numbers: Experiment 1: 106 recruited, 5 excluded and replaced for finding the rule in the first session. Sleep group 59 percent (13 of 22) gained insight. Each of the four other groups had 5 solvers (5/22 = 22.7 percent or 5/20 = 25 percent). Global test chi2 = 10.2, df = 4, p = .03. Groups: 8 h night sleep, 8 h night wake, 8 h day wake, and two morning/evening groups of 20.
limits: Closes the Wagner part of gap 5. Global p = .03 is modest and cells are 20-22 people. The same lab reports it did not reproduce the high solution rate in later work.
agent_relevance: Rule discovery after an offline pass is real but rests on tiny cells (13 of 22). Treat the sleep gain as roughly +35 points with wide error, not as a solid effect size.

source: Verleger et al. (2013) same paper: Experiments 2-3, slow-wave sleep and prior implicit knowledge
finding: The sleep benefit for insight was specific to people who had already acquired the hidden regularity implicitly before sleep, and was linked to slow-wave sleep and 10-12 Hz EEG power.
numbers: Abstract: sleep triples insight above a base rate of about 20 percent; a hard core of about 20 percent discoverers differed in EEG from the start (Experiment 2, 26 participants analysed).
limits: Own-lab, small samples, exploratory EEG, moderator found post hoc.
agent_relevance: Offline abstraction pays most when the raw episodes already hold a partial trace of the rule. An agent should consolidate episodes that show recurring structure, not all episodes.

source: Schonauer, Brodt, Pohlchen, Bressmer, Danek, Gais (2018) Sleep does not promote solving classical insight problems and magic tricks
finding: With 77 people, no sleep benefit for classical insight problems or magic tricks, and none for solutions with a felt moment of insight. The authors list partial or failed number-reduction replications: Debarnot 2017 (benefit in young but not older adults) and a later Wagner-lab study that did not reproduce the high post-sleep solution rate.
numbers: N = 77. Retest gain on magic tricks 1.40 +/- 0.13 tricks; sleep effect F(1,64) = 0.047, p = .829, partial eta2 = .001; incubation effect F(1,64) = 0.008, p = .930. Sessions spaced 3 h apart (sleep or wake).
limits: Different tasks from the number reduction task. Three-hour sleep window is short. Debarnot and Verleger details are second-hand here.
agent_relevance: Rule or insight discovery from sleep depends on the task. Do not assume an abstraction pass finds new rules in every domain.

source: Lacaux, Izabelle, Santantonio, De Villele et al. (2021) Sleep onset is a creative sweet spot (Science Advances)
finding: A nap study found the gain came from the lightest sleep stage (N1), not slow-wave sleep. At least 15 s in N1 tripled the chance of finding a hidden rule; deeper sleep removed the effect.
numbers: N = 103. Discovery of the hidden rule 83 percent with at least 15 s of N1 versus 30 percent for those who stayed awake. Effect vanished if participants reached deeper sleep.
limits: Subgroups defined by the stage reached, not randomised. Opposite stage result to d05.
agent_relevance: Challenges the idea that deep-sleep replay is what finds rules. Hints a loose, low-constraint pass may serve rule finding better than strict replay.

source: Lowe, Petzka, Tzegka, Schuck (2025) N2 sleep promotes the occurrence of aha moments in a perceptual insight task (PLOS Biology, preregistered)
finding: A preregistered nap study (N = 90) found N2 sleep, not N1, raised insight. This contradicts Lacaux 2021 on the stage. The paper itself says earlier evidence is mixed and cites studies with no sleep benefit.
numbers: 90 enrolled; 68 in the insight analysis (28 reached N2, 22 only N1, 18 stayed awake). Insight ratio 85.7 percent (N2) vs 55.5 percent (wake); N1 63.6 percent not different from the others. Baseline insight ratio with no nap 49.5 percent. 70.6 percent (48/68) classed as insight subjects overall.
limits: 20-minute daytime nap, perceptual decision task, not a number rule. Groups defined by sleep reached, not randomised.
agent_relevance: Best current preregistered result: some sleep helps, but the active stage is unsettled (N1 in one lab, N2 in another). Do not copy a stage into the agent design.

source: Beijamini, Valentin, Jager, Born, Diekelmann (2021) Sleep facilitates problem solving with no additional gain through targeted memory reactivation
finding: Sleep helped solve a game-based puzzle, and more SWS predicted success, but cueing the puzzle during sleep added nothing.
numbers: Experiment 1: 62 percent solved after sleep vs 24 percent after wake (about 10 h). Experiment 2 (TMR): 56 percent (SWS cues), 58 percent (REM cues), 57 percent (wake cues).
limits: Group sizes not extracted from the abstract; same lab family as the theory (Born, Diekelmann).
agent_relevance: Natural offline processing gave the whole gain; targeted replay of chosen items added nothing. Mirrors gap 7: choosing what to replay may not help.

source: Vickrey and Lerner (2023) Overnight exposure to pink noise could jeopardize sleep-dependent insight and pattern detection
finding: Pink noise, a known memory enhancer, did not raise insight in the number reduction task and looked closer to the wake condition. Time in the first N1 stretch predicted insight.
numbers: 72 participants analysed (87 recruited) in three groups: daytime wake, silent sleep, sleep with pink noise; 12 h between sessions; DREEM headband at home.
limits: Open-loop noise, at-home recording, small groups. Uses the Wagner task but is not a direct replication.
agent_relevance: Stimulation that helps retention can harm rule discovery. A replay boost for recall may not carry over to rule finding in an agent.

source: Lerner and Gluck (2019) Sleep and the extraction of hidden regularities: a systematic review and the importance of temporal rules (Sleep Medicine Reviews)
finding: Many null results. Which task was used mattered more than the cognitive process or the design. Explicit rule detection was more likely for temporal rules (event A predicts later event B) than non-temporal rules.
numbers: Abstract only (full text not retrievable); no pooled effect size in the abstract.
limits: Abstract-level reading of a review, not a new test.
agent_relevance: Suggests offline consolidation works best on sequence and temporal regularities, which is what agent episodes are. Supports sequence-aware rule extraction.

source: Wunderlin, Zeller, Klinzing et al. (2021) Modulating overnight memory consolidation by acoustic stimulation during slow-wave sleep: systematic review and meta-analysis (Sleep)
finding: Acoustic enhancement of slow waves gives a small, borderline memory gain. The authors do not recommend commercial devices.
numbers: 10 studies, 11 experiments, 177 participants. Hedges g = 0.25, p = 0.07. Subgroups: young adults g = 0.31 (p = 0.051), phase-locked g = 0.36 (p = 0.047), both g = 0.44 (p = 0.01, n = 6). No publication bias flagged.
limits: Read from the Europe PMC abstract record only. Few small studies. Search date October 2020.
agent_relevance: Supports Cordi and Rasch's cautious reading: stimulating the replay machinery gives small effects, so the human mechanism is a weak design lever.

source: Stanyer et al. (2022) The impact of acoustic stimulation during sleep on memory and sleep architecture: a meta-analysis (J Sleep Res), RETRACTED 2026
finding: A 2022 meta-analysis that had reported a large acoustic-stimulation effect on declarative memory in young adults was retracted in 2026 after the authors found errors that make its conclusions invalid.
numbers: Original claim (now invalid): g = 0.68 in under-35s, g = 0.87 for declarative tasks, 16 studies. Retraction notice: standard error used in place of standard deviation, and incorrect sample sizes.
limits: Retraction notice read in the Europe PMC record. Do not cite the 2022 numbers.
agent_relevance: Drop any citation of a large acoustic-stimulation effect from this paper. Only the 2021 Sleep meta-analysis (g = 0.25) stands.

source: Hausdorf, Ferdinand, Koo-Poeggel, Molle, Bazhenov, Marshall (2025) Stimulating the stimulated cortex: frontocortical anodal tDCS with closed-loop acoustic stimulation during sleep (Eur J Neurosci, PMC12493016)
finding: Adding anodal tDCS to closed-loop sound did not change overall overnight memory. Memory fell only in people with higher fluid intelligence. Sleep efficiency and late-night REM fell. So the earlier snippet 'stimulation impaired memory' is a subgroup result.
numbers: 20 participants (18-30), two nights: CLAS alone vs tDCS + CLAS. No memory difference across all subjects. Slow oscillations shifted negative and lengthened, density fell. High-Raven subgroup retention significantly lower after combined stimulation.
limits: N = 20 within-subject; subgroup found by splitting on Raven score (probably not preregistered). Compares CLAS+tDCS with CLAS, not with sham, so it says nothing on whether CLAS alone works.
agent_relevance: Not a refutation of replay; a warning that boosting the process can disturb it. Any tuning of an agent consolidation pass should be tested for harm elsewhere, not only for gain.

source: Aksamaz, Molle, Akinola, Gromodka, Bazhenov, Marshall (2024) Single closed-loop acoustic stimulation targeting memory consolidation suppressed hippocampal ripple and thalamocortical spindle activity in mice (PMC11214843)
finding: In mice, closed-loop sound at four slow-oscillation phases did not improve object-place memory over sham. Up-state stimulation did beat stimulation at one other phase. Every stimulus gave a ripple burst followed by about a second of ripple suppression and longer spindle suppression.
numbers: 3-hour retention interval; no significant improvement over sham; up-state retention higher than one other phase; ripple suppression about 1 s; NREM duration unchanged.
limits: Mouse study with single pulses, not the human pulse-train protocols. Sample sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Mechanistic reason timing matters and a replay boost can interrupt the replay it targets. In agent terms: extra rehearsal at the wrong moment can disrupt real work.

source: Closed-loop auditory stimulation nulls: chronic insomnia crossover (medRxiv 10.1101/2025.03.04.25321710) and ecological-setting study (J Sleep Res 2026, 10.1111/jsr.70247)
finding: Two more closed-loop auditory stimulation studies raised slow-oscillation amplitude but found no memory benefit.
numbers: Insomnia: N = 27 randomised sham-controlled crossover, no effect on sleep or on declarative memory (word pairs). Home study: N = 34 between groups, one stimulated night, no memory or vigilance effect; authors say the sample may be too small.
limits: Abstract records only. Small N. Does not include the Henin follow-ups, which I could not retrieve.
agent_relevance: Adds nulls to the Cordi and Rasch 2021 list. Gap 6: the robustness reading is slightly weaker, not changed. Henin follow-ups specifically stay unchecked.

source: Ye et al. (2026) Auto-Dreamer: Learning Offline Memory Consolidation for Language Agents, Table 2 and cadence sweep (arXiv 2605.20616)
finding: The best ablation of what an offline pass does. Rewriting memory regions with no training already cut bank size 6-11x and raised success in all three domains; RL training added more on two of three. Consolidation cadence shows an inverted U: too frequent and too rare both hurt.
numbers: Success rate (SR) / memory-bank tokens. ALFWorld: writer-only 48.0 / 50,735; untrained consolidator 59.2 / 6,900; trained 60.2 / 10,954. ScienceWorld: 29.6 / 61,679; 31.4 / 5,700; 41.1 / 6,947. WebArena: 44.2 / 6,421; 46.6 / 1,067; 52.3 / 927. Cadence k in {1,5,20} vs main (k = 8 ALFWorld, 10 ScienceWorld): main beat both on ScienceWorld; ALFWorld range about 5 pp, k = 5 was +1.1 pp. Provenance fan-in peaks at 5 source entries per synthesized entry.
limits: Retrieval is capped (top-K = 3 with a token cap), so query-time tokens are about equal, but the consolidator's own token cost is not reported in the tables I read. Limitations section: point estimates, no seed or task-order variance. ScienceWorld cadence numbers are in a figure only.
agent_relevance: Answers gaps 1, 2, 4 in part. Writer-only vs consolidated at capped retrieval is a fair query-side control, not an equal-total-token control. Region size per pass is the only LLM data on a capacity limit.

source: Ye et al. (2026) Auto-Dreamer, Appendix H bootstrap CIs and baselines (arXiv 2605.20616)
finding: Rule-extraction baselines (ExpeL, AWM, Memp, ReasoningBank) sit close to no memory on ScienceWorld; the new consolidator is the only one clearly above. These CIs reflect task sampling only, not seeds.
numbers: Bootstrap 95 percent CIs (10,000 resamples over tasks). ScienceWorld: no memory 28.69, ExpeL 28.33, AWM 30.18, Memp 30.36, ReasoningBank 30.86, Auto-Dreamer 41.07 [37.53, 44.70]. ALFWorld: no memory 30.83, Reflexion 49.17 [43.59, 54.73], ExpeL 33.59, Auto-Dreamer 60.21 [54.65, 65.59] (nearly touches Reflexion). WebArena: no memory 44.6, ExpeL 50.8, Auto-Dreamer 52.3 [43.5, 60.9] (overlaps all).
limits: Task-resampling noise only, as the limitations admit. Qwen-class models, three text environments. Corrects the earlier note: CIs exist, seed variance does not.
agent_relevance: ExpeL-style insight lists gave about zero gain over no memory in two of three environments. Do not assume rule extraction helps by default; test it against no-memory on your own tasks.

source: Lv et al. (2026) All-Mem: Agentic Lifelong Memory via Dynamic Topology Evolution, ablations and cost (arXiv 2603.19595)
finding: Offline merge/split/update of memory units, with raw units kept, improves LoCoMo and LongMemEval-s at matched query-time budget. Ablations separate merging (dedup) from recovery of archived raw evidence. Dropping Merge costs about 3 F1 points.
numbers: LoCoMo (4o-judge / F1 / R@5): full 54.63 / 52.18 / 46.63; no visibility control 50.87 / 47.63 / 41.84; without Merge 52.08 / 49.02 / 43.96; anchors only (no recovery) 51.76 / 49.27 / 43.19; no recovery links 52.74 / 50.06 / 44.07. LongMemEval-s: 60.20 judge, 45.19 F1; +4.40 and +9.09 over Mem0. Cost: online 539 tokens/turn; query 918 tokens; offline event 74.1k tokens, amortized 1,237 tokens/turn.
limits: Query-time budgets matched with Mem0 (about 1.4-2.1k tokens) but the offline 1,237 tokens/turn, more than the online 539, is not matched against a baseline that spends it elsewhere. Single runs; no seeds in the sections read.
agent_relevance: Strongest published fixed-budget ablation of dedup and of source-linked recovery. Shows the offline pass costs more tokens than writing the memory, which a fair control must charge. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Lv et al. (2026) All-Mem Appendices G-H: reachability and human audit of consolidation edits
finding: Keeping archived raw units reachable by links makes consolidation edits mostly safe. A hand audit of 190 accepted edits found most correct and few harmful; the typical harm is merging units that share an entity but hold different facts.
numbers: Audit: Split 40 edits, 90.0 percent valid, 5.0 percent harmful; Merge 80 edits, 93.8 percent valid, 3.8 percent harmful; Update 70 edits, 95.7 percent valid, 2.9 percent harmful; all 190 edits 94.2 percent valid, 3.7 percent harmful. 0 percent of archived units unreachable; median 2 hops; 95 percent coverage within 4 hops.
limits: Edit correctness only, not downstream answer quality; only confidence-gated and validated edits; one annotation protocol.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 in part: source-linked raw evidence stops edits being destructive, at the price of a link-following step at query time. Remaining risk is silent over-merging.

source: Dai et al. (2026) RecMem: Recurrence-based Memory Consolidation (arXiv 2605.16045), results and ablation
finding: Deferring LLM abstraction until a topic recurs cuts construction tokens about 87 percent versus eager consolidators with little accuracy loss. Keeping raw interactions in a first tier is the largest contributor. Full context still wins on short LoCoMo.
numbers: LoCoMo GPT-4.1-mini construction tokens: 193.2K vs Mem0 1520.8K (-87.3 percent) and A-Mem 1459.9K (-86.8 percent). Overall score (garbled table; columns read as Full context, Naive RAG, MemoryOS, Mem0, A-Mem, RecMem): 90.84, 61.24, 77.05, 66.23, 73.25, 86.92. GPT-4o-mini overall: 76.43, 49.68, 63.64, 58.64, 60.84, 72.47; temporal RecMem 57.32 vs A-Mem 61.99. Ablation (GPT-4.1-mini, full 81.10): without raw tier 51.88; without semantic tier 70.58; without episodic tier 79.94; direct extraction without recurrence gating 74.22 (label position read from the figure). Thresholds sim 0.7 / count 5 (LoCoMo); scores averaged over three runs.
limits: Gating is bundled with the three-tier design, so 74.22 vs 81.10 mixes gating and tiers. Table and figure text garbled; order inferred. Full context beats RecMem on LoCoMo (about 16K-token chats). Offline cost is charged here, the best equal-cost view so far.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gaps 2 and 7: recurrence gating is the only replay-selection rule with an LLM ablation, worth about 7 points over direct extraction; the raw tier is worth about 29 points.

source: Kerestecioglu, Robsky, Vasters, Sharma et al. (2026) Human-inspired memory architecture for LLM agents, LongMemEval S-tier ablation (arXiv 2605.08538)
finding: Nine-configuration ablation with bootstrap CIs. Deduplication at moderate budget is statistically no worse than raw RAG. Merging turns into cluster summaries is badly destructive. The authors conclude: consolidate by deduplicating, not summarizing. Their consolidation code runs no LLM calls.
numbers: LongMemEval S-tier (500 questions), overall accuracy [95 percent CI]: raw RAG 78.4 [74.8, 82.0]; dedup-only 76.8 [73.0, 80.4]; dedup + reconsolidation 75.8 [72.0, 79.6]; adaptive 10K budget 57.0 [52.8, 61.4]; aggressive cluster-merge 48.4 [44.0, 52.8]; aggressive + reconsolidation 48.8 [44.4, 53.4]. Single-session assistant questions fell from 94.6 to 39.3 under aggressive merge. Preference questions 56.7 to 70.0 with dedup (30 questions, not significant). VSCode stream: 97.2 percent retention precision, 58 percent store reduction, +21.8 pp over keep-everything (75.4).
limits: Embedding-based deterministic consolidation, not LLM abstraction. Thresholds calibrated on synthetic data. One run per configuration.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gaps 2, 3 and 10: dedup is safe, hard forgetting hurts, summarizing clusters destroys details, reconsolidation adds nothing measurable (CI fully overlaps dedup-only).

source: Kerestecioglu et al. (2026) same paper: LongMemEval M-tier (475 sessions) token-budget sweep
finding: At very long histories the consolidated store only matches raw retrieval at a 200K-token budget; smaller budgets lose facts. The paper claims the value is a tunable trade-off, not higher accuracy.
numbers: M-tier overall accuracy [95 percent CI]: raw RAG (k = 10) 71.2 [67.2, 75.0]; pipeline at 200K tokens 70.1 [66.0, 74.2]; 115K 65.6 [61.4, 69.6]; 50K 49.2 [44.8, 53.6]; 25K 38.8 [34.6, 43.2] (pairing of CIs to budgets inferred from a garbled table). Pipeline +1.2 pp on multi-session and +3.0 pp on temporal reasoning (directional).
limits: Table partly garbled. Baseline is simple RAG, not a fixed-total-token control. Reconsolidation was on in all M-tier configurations.
agent_relevance: Fixed budgets show a cross-over: below about 115K-200K tokens the compaction hurts rather than helps. Compaction trades facts for tokens.

source: Zhao, Cao et al. (2026) RPMem: recurrent parametric memory across sessions (arXiv 2609.23466), consolidation-rule ablation
finding: A learned write gate that decides how much of each new session to merge beats every fixed merge rule tried. Keeping every session adapter without selection collapses.
numbers: Qwen3-8B on PERMA: learned gate 85.52 percent; the strongest fixed rule (LoRA factor averaging) is 31.31 pp lower; latent averaging 8.04 pp worse than keeping only the latest session; factor averaging only +0.65 pp over latest session; rank concatenation (keep all) 13.84 percent. Gate gain over factor averaging 21.45 pp (single-domain), 41.16 pp (multi-domain).
limits: Parametric (LoRA) memory that needs training, not a text scaffold. The gate is task-trained, so part of the gain is benchmark-family training.
agent_relevance: Selective integration matters when sessions are heterogeneous. Supports a selection rule in a scaffold, but this paper does not test text-level replay selection.
